title: Reaching a Consensus in Predictive Loops
claim: Predictive systems and individuals form a feedback loop: platform predictions shape opinions, peers reshape them, and the resulting data retrains the platform.
layout: 3 labeled stages in a cycle, left to right, with a return arrow
description: A cyclic diagram of a platform-people feedback loop. On the left, a rounded gray box labeled 'AI platform' holds a small neural-network icon in a dashed frame and the caption 'model updates'. Three orange curved arrows labeled (A) 'platform influence' run from the box to a large rounded blue-gray panel on the right. The panel holds two social-network graphs, drawn as gray edges with nodes in shades of blue. The left graph has a wide spread of dark and light nodes. The right graph has nodes of more uniform mid-blue. A thick blue arrow labeled (B) 'peer influence' joins the two graphs. A long green curved arrow labeled (C) 'data collection' returns from the network to the platform box. Small laptop and person icons with double-headed arrows show the interactions. Circled red letters A, B and C mark the steps. The eye goes first to the networks, then follows the arrows around the loop.
caption: Peer-platform co-influence in opinion dynamics: (A) Individuals interact with a digital platform that deploys a predictive system and update their opinions based on the content they are exposed to. (B) Individuals' opinions evolve through peer interaction. (C) Expressed opinions inform future platform predictions.
abstract: Predictions in digital platforms must adapt over time as individuals update their beliefs through social interactions. At the same time, changing predictions alter the content people are exposed to and, consequently, the very beliefs they aim to forecast. This recursive coupling between predictions and individuals complicates the analysis of the long-term societal impact of predictive systems. In this work, we propose a minimal model where predictions and opinions co-evolve, combining insights from network science with concepts from performative prediction. In our model a platform's predictions influence individual opinions, which then evolve through peer interactions and form the training data for future platform model updates. We demonstrate that this co-evolution induces a novel equilibrium that qualitatively differs from standard network equilibria. In particular, we show how standard predictive objectives can drive networks toward consensus even under conditions where classical opinion-dynamics models lead to disagreement. This emerges because predictive systems dynamically adapt to changing opinions, and learning objectives create spillover effects among individuals beyond the topology of the network. We further analyze systematic deviations from standard prediction and demonstrate amplified effects of targeted platform interventions on equilibrium outcomes, compared to classical network intervention analyses. Together, our results illustrate performativity as an important, yet so far neglected, qualifying factor in social networks.
